Anomalous Tunneling Systems in Amorphous Organic Materials

S. Sahling Affiliation: Institut für Festkörperphysik, TU Dresden, 01062 Dresden, Germany    M. Koláč Affiliation: Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic    V.L. Katkov Email: katkov@theor.jinr.ru Affiliation: Bogoliubov Laboratory of Theoretical Physics, Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, 141980 Dubna, Moscow region, Russia    V.A. Osipov Affiliation: Bogoliubov Laboratory of Theoretical Physics, Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, 141980 Dubna, Moscow region, Russia
Abstract

We compare the heat release data of organic glasses with that of amorphous and glass like crystalline solids. Anomalous behavior was found in all these materials, which disagrees with the standard tunneling model. We can explain the most of the experimental observations within a phenomenological model, where we assume that for a part of tunneling systems the barrier heights are strongly reduced as a consequence of the local stress produced during the cooling process.

I Introduction

Let us begin with an overview of the main results and conclusions concerning the heat capacity and heat release experiments in inorganic and glasslike crystalline materials. It has been recently shown that barrier heights of two-level systems (TLSs) in both amorphous and glasslike crystalline solids can be drastically reduced by frozen in local mechanical stresses caused by a rapid cooling of the sample [1]. The value of the reduction can be estimated in the framework of Eyring model [2] that is widely employed for describing stress-induced yielding and non-linear mechanical response in polymer glasses [3]. Strong local fluctuations of the stress are expected to exist in glasses and the maximum barrier height Vm​a​xV_{max} is reduced to Vam​a​xV_{a}^{max} after the cooling of the sample with Vm​a​x−Vam​a​x=σm​a​x​Va​cV^{max}-V^{max}_{a}=\sigma^{max}V_{ac} where Va​cV_{ac} is a so-called activation volume (a typical volume required for a molecular shear rearrangement) and σ\sigma is the frozen in stress caused by the thermal expansion. As a consequence, the distribution of the barrier heights becomes much more complicated than that assumed within the standard tunneling model (STM) [4, 5], which gives roughly a constant distribution P⁡(V)=P0P(V)=P_{0}. Namely, there appears a step in the distribution function at Vam​a​xV_{a}^{max} (see Fig. 1). Moreover, the relaxation time of the tunneling process also exhibits a step at the corresponding relaxation time τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}.

In the one-phonon approximation, the relaxation rate of a thermally activated process is written as

τt−1=A⁡(E​Δ02/kB3)​coth⁡(E/2​kB​T).\tau_{t}^{-1}=A(E\Delta_{0}^{2}/k_{B}^{3})\coth(E/2k_{B}T). (1)

One gets τt=τam​a​x\tau_{t}=\tau_{a}^{max} at Δ0=Δ0m​i​n\Delta_{0}=\Delta_{0}^{min} where the minimum tunneling energy

Δ0m​i​n=(2E0/π)exp(−Vam​a​x/E0),\Delta_{0}^{min}=(2E_{0}/\pi)\exp(-V_{a}^{max}/E_{0}), (2)

E0E_{0} is the zero-point energy [6], and

A=8​π3​kB3ρ​h4​(γl2υl5+γt2υt5).A=\frac{8\pi^{3}k_{B}^{3}}{\rho h^{4}}\left(\frac{\gamma_{l}^{2}}{\upsilon^{5}_{l}}+\frac{\gamma_{t}^{2}}{\upsilon^{5}_{t}}\right). (3)

TLSs with the reduced barrier heights were called anomalous (aTLSs). The results agree well with the predictions of the STM for all parameters when the experimental time scale tt is less than τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}. For example, in vitreous silica τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} is found to be of the order of 100100 s, and the spectral density obtained from the heat capacity (PCP_{C}), thermal conductivity, ultrasound, damping (internal friction) agree quite well with the STM [7]. However, the heat release was measured at longer time up to 10510^{5} s and for t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max} gives a spectral density PQP_{Q} roughly 44 times smaller than the spectral density PCP_{C} deduced from the heat capacity. One can estimate the value of the step as (Pa+Pn)/Pn=PC/PQ(P_{a}+P_{n})/P_{n}=P_{C}/P_{Q}, where a small contribution of anomalous TLSs to the heat release at t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max} (Pa​0P_{a0} in Fig. 1) has been neglected (explanation see below). We get Pa/Pn=3P_{a}/P_{n}=3 for vitreous silica, which means that the main part of TLSs is anomalous [7]. It should be stressed that the most of thermodynamical parameters taken from experiments do not allow us to distinguish between the contribution of normal and anomalous TLSs, while this is possible by the heat release measurements.

The heat capacity experiment yields the spectral density PCP_{C}, which is an average value of all tunneling systems between τm​i​n\tau^{min} and tt, where τm​i​n\tau^{min} is the minimum relaxation time of the TLSs and tt is the time of the heat capacity measurement (typically, t∼1t\sim 1 s). Thus, the heat capacity always gives the spectral density for t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max}, that is PC=Pa+PnP_{C}=P_{a}+P_{n}.

The heat release is caused by TLSs with the relaxation time close to the measuring time tt (numerical calculations with a standard distribution function show that the heat release at the time tt is produced by TLSs with the relaxation time t/10<τt<20​tt/10<\tau_{t}<20t). Their corresponding barrier heights are located in a quite small range Δ​V≈(0.1−0.2)​Vm\Delta V\approx(0.1-0.2)V_{m}, where VmV_{m} is an average value, which determines the relaxation time τt=t\tau_{t}=t. Thus, the heat release experiments give us the spectral density for a well-defined barrier height VmV_{m} and, therefore, by increasing time one can move from the left to the right side of the step in the distribution P⁡(V)P(V). Notice that the new parameter τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} plays an important role in our model. Namely, in accordance with Fig. 1 we get different results for both the heat release and its correlation to the heat capacity in three different regions:

  1. 1.

    Vm<Vam​a​xV_{m}<V_{a}^{max} and t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max}

  2. 2.

    Vm=Vam​a​xV_{m}=V_{a}^{max} and t=τam​a​xt=\tau_{a}^{max}

  3. 3.

    Vm>Vam​a​xV_{m}>V_{a}^{max} and t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max}

In the first region we reproduce the results of the STM with a new spectral density P=Pa+Pn=PC=PQP=P_{a}+P_{n}=P_{C}=P_{Q}. Explicitly,

Cp=(π2​kB2/12)​PC​T​ln⁡(4​t/τm​i​n),C_{p}=(\pi^{2}k_{B}^{2}/12)P_{C}T\ln(4t/\tau^{min}), (4)

where τm​i​n=τt​(Δ0=E)\tau^{min}=\tau_{t}(\Delta_{0}=E), and

d​Q/d​t≡Q˙=(π2​kB2/24)​PQ​Vs​(T12−T02)​t−1,dQ/dt\equiv\dot{Q}=(\pi^{2}k_{B}^{2}/24)P_{Q}V_{s}(T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2})t^{-1}, (5)

with VsV_{s} being the volume of the sample, T1T_{1} the starting, and T0T_{0} the final temperature. At low temperatures (T0T_{0}, T1<Tc​0T_{1}<T_{c0}), for the heat release we found no difference from the STM. Here Tc​0T_{c0} is the crossover temperature, where the relaxation rate of the tunneling τt−1\tau_{t}^{-1} is equal to the relaxation rate of the thermally activated process. Above the crossover temperature the relaxation time of normal TLSs decreases rapidly with increasing temperature due to the Arrhenius law. As a consequence, a part of TLSs relaxes during the cooling process and does not contribute to the heat release. In this case, the heat release deviates from T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} behavior. At high enough temperatures T1>T∗T_{1}>T^{*} (T∗T^{*} is the freezing temperature), all TLSs with the energy E>2.4​kB​T∗E>2.4k_{B}T^{*} reach the state of equilibrium during the cooling process, and the heat release saturates. Thus a maximum value of the heat release will be observed at T1≈T∗T_{1}\approx T^{*} in Eq. (5). T∗T^{*} depends weekly on the cooling rate R∗R^{*} at this temperature and is directly proportional to the barrier height VmV_{m} of the TLSs causing the heat release at given time after the cooling to a temperature T0<Tc​0T_{0}<T_{c0}. Notice that the freezing temperature is close to the crossover temperature Tn∗≈1.2​Tc​0T_{n}^{*}\approx 1.2T_{c0} for normal TLSs (see [8]). However, the barrier height of anomalous TLSs increases with increasing temperature and their freezing temperature Ta∗T^{*}_{a} can be essentially higher than Tn∗T_{n}^{*}. In this case, a giant heat release will be observed since the heat release saturates at very high temperatures T1=Ta∗T_{1}=T^{*}_{a} .

In the second region, the heat release relaxes very fast and can be described by the relation

Q˙=[Ql+(Qs−Ql)exp(−t/τam​a​x)]t−1,\dot{Q}=[Q_{l}+(Q_{s}-Q_{l})\exp(-t/\tau_{a}^{max})]t^{-1}, (6)

where QlQ_{l} and QsQ_{s} are proportional to Pa​0+PnP_{a0}+P_{n} and Pa+PnP_{a}+P_{n}, respectively. In the heat release one can directly see the step in the distribution function and determine the maximum relaxation time of anomalous TLSs as a function of an average energy Ea​v/kB=2.4​(T1+T0)/2E_{av}/k_{B}=2.4(T_{1}+T_{0})/2. This rare case was observed in ZrCaO [9]. Fig. 2 shows the heat release as a function of time after cooling from different T1T_{1} to T0=1.3T_{0}=1.3 K.

Notice that Eq. (6) describes the time dependence very well. Fig. 3 shows the energy dependence of τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}, where we point out another interesting fact: the maximum energy is not proportional to 1/Ea​v1/E_{av}, as expected from the STM (see Eq. (1)) but roughly proportional to Ea​v≈T1+T0E_{av}\approx T_{1}+T_{0}.

In the region 3 there is a remarkable discrepancy between PCP_{C} and PQP_{Q} since

PCPQ=Pa+PnPa​0+Pn>1.\frac{P_{C}}{P_{Q}}=\frac{P_{a}+P_{n}}{P_{a0}+P_{n}}>1. (7)

In this case, the heat release is mainly determined by the normal TLSs, and the maximum heat release is much smaller than the value measured at t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max}. Nevertheless, there is also a small contribution of anomalous TLSs (Pa​0P_{a0} in Fig. 1). It was suggested that this small contribution to the heat release at t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max} could be caused by some distribution of the local stresses in the sample after a rapid cooling. Within this scenario, the maximum local stress will reduce Vm​a​xV^{max} to Vam​a​xV_{a}^{max} after the cooling. For smaller stress, the corresponding VV will take the values between Vam​a​xV_{a}^{max} and Vm​a​xV^{max} at the relaxation time t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max}, and a corresponding freezing temperature T∗T^{*} varies between Tn∗<T∗<Ta∗T^{*}_{n}<T^{*}<T^{*}_{a}. Thus, the distribution of the local stresses leads to a contribution of anomalous TLSs at t>τam​a​xt>\tau_{a}^{max}. Such a contribution was observed in all materials with PC>PQP_{C}>P_{Q}. Notice that Pa​0P_{a0} is small in comparison to PaP_{a} - for example, Pa​0/Pa=0.05P_{a0}/P_{a}=0.05 for vitrous silica [7]. Nevertheless, for high initial temperatures this fraction of anomalous TLSs gives the dominant contribution to the heat release (roughly 2 times larger than the contribution of normal TLSs) since they have also a much higher Ta​0∗T^{*}_{a0} in comparison to Tn∗T^{*}_{n} (see Fig. 4).

Measuring the T1T_{1}-dependence of the heat release one can separate the contribution of normal and anomalous TLSs. Fig. 4 shows the parameter Q1=t​Q˙Q_{1}=t\dot{Q} as a function of T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2}. The contribution of normal TLSs saturates for a-SiO2 at Tn∗=5.5T^{*}_{n}=5.5 K while for anomalous TLSs (Pa​0P_{a0}) it saturates above 14.114.1 K. Values of these two contributions are proportional to PnP_{n} and Pa​0P_{a0}, correspondingly. τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} depends on the values of local stresses and Vm​a​xV^{max} as well as on the mass of tunneling entity. The last possibility was demonstrated for TLSs in NbTi caused by H or D in [1].

The heat release and heat capacity data of all investigated inorganic amorphous and glasslike crystalline solids complies with one of these three cases (see Table 1). A transition between cases one and three is rarely observed since changing measuring time in the heat release experiments by a factor of ten modifies the corresponding barrier height by a few percents only. All three cases were observed in ZrO2CaO [9] (see Fig. 2), PLZT [10] and also in a-SiO2 [7] and NbTi-H [1].

It should be noted that the heat release in amorphous organic materials has not yet been analysed in detail. At the same time, the experimental studies of organic glasses show a rather specific behavior of the heat release. In this paper, we make a comparison of the heat capacity and heat release data between organic glasses, inorganic glasses, and glasslike crystalline materials. Our analysis clearly indicates the existence of anomalous TLSs in all these materials; their possible origin is the local stresses during the cooling process.

II Heat capacity and heat release of amorphous organic materials

Our purpose is to analyse the relevant heat release and heat capacity data for organic amorphous materials and show that anomalous TLSs should also exist in these materials. If this is the case, the distribution function must be similar to that in inorganic glasses with a step at Vam​a​xV_{a}^{max}. There is, however, an important difference: in organic materials the heat release decays as t−at^{-a} with a<1a<1 in contrast to both the predictions of STM and the t−1t^{-1} behavior observed in most of inorganic glasses. As a possible explanation one can assume an additional strong increase of P⁡(τ)P(\tau) near τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}. Let us consider an extreme case of a δ\delta-like growth. In this case, the heat release should be written as

Q˙=Qn/t+Q˙a\dot{Q}=Q_{n}/t+\dot{Q}_{a} (8)

with

Q˙a=[Qa/t+Pa​x]exp(−t/τam​a​x),\dot{Q}_{a}=\left[Q_{a}/t+P_{ax}\right]\exp(-t/\tau_{a}^{max}), (9)

where Pa​xP_{ax} is a time independent contribution to the heat release. Otherwise, we would expect to find for PQP_{Q} a value larger or close to PCP_{C} for t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max}, and a fast relaxation of the heat release at t≈τam​a​xt\approx\tau_{a}^{max}.

II.1 Heat capacity and heat release of PMMA

One of the first long time heat release experiments were performed by Zimmermann and Weber with a-SiO2 and PMMA [11, 12]. In both materials the poor agreement with the STM was observed. The results of vitreous silica were considered and discussed in detail in ref. [7]. The results of PMMA are shown in Fig. 5. For low T1T_{1}, the heat release is roughly proportional to t−1t^{-1} as predicted by the STM. However, a markedly different time dependence was observed for higher T1T_{1}.

A much better agreement we get with a fit

Q˙=(Q1/t+Pa​x)exp(−t/τam​a​x),\dot{Q}=(Q_{1}/t+P_{ax})\exp(-t/\tau_{a}^{max}), (10)

where

Q1=Qa+Qn.Q_{1}=Q_{a}+Q_{n}. (11)

The heat release of PMMA is at low temperatures T1T_{1} and short time mainly determined by the term Ql/tQ_{l}/t and agrees here quite well with the STM. However, Eq. (10) yields a much better agreement with the experimental data including that data at higher T1T_{1} and long time. As is seen, that Eq. (10) differs from Eqs. (8) and (9): the exponent cuts down also QnQ_{n}, and therefore this fit fails at t≫τam​a​xt\gg\tau_{a}^{max}. In order to separate terms QaQ_{a} and QnQ_{n} we need the heat release data either for higher temperatures T1T_{1} or for t≫τam​a​xt\gg\tau_{a}^{max}. Unfortunately, they are not yet available for PMMA. As we see in Fig. 4, T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} dependence of Q1Q_{1} agrees with the STM. Thus, we can estimate the distribution parameter by using the STM. The result is PQ=28×1044P_{Q}=28\times 10^{44} Jm3 at ρ=1.19\rho=1.19 g/cm3. Notice that this parameter really markedly exceeds the value deduced from the heat capacity PC=8.4×1044P_{C}=8.4\times 10^{44} Jm3 [13]. This finding indicates that the heat release is strongly influenced by the new term Pa​xP_{ax} which is also strongly proportional to T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} (see Fig. 6). This means that all contributions to the heat release have the same or similar distribution function of the energy (P⁡(E)=c​o​n​s​tP(E)=const).

Notice that the increase of the distribution function with VV could explain the deviation from t−1t^{-1} behavior of the heat release. However, in this case we would obtain a deviation from T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} behavior as well. In particular, the model with TLS-TLS interaction taken into account gives P∼1/Δ02P\sim 1/\Delta_{0}^{2} [14]. This function was successfully used to fit the data of spectral diffusion in PMMA [15]. However, using this distribution function in our case we obiain Q˙∼T15/2−T05/2\dot{Q}\sim T_{1}^{5/2}-T_{0}^{5/2}, which is inconsistent with the heat release experimental data (see Fig. 4).

The contribution of the anomalous TLSs and normal TLSs cannot be separated because this requires the heat release experiments with higher T1T_{1} which were not performed up to now.

II.2 Heat release of 3-MP/2,3-DMB

Heat release measurements were performed with 3-methylpentane/2,3-dimethylbutan at much higher starting temperature than for PMMA (up to 20 K) [16]. The heat release is found to be roughly proportional to t−0.7t^{-0.7} and relaxes much faster for a very long time (see Fig. 7). Notice that even a sharp cut of the TLSs distribution function could not provoke such strong dying in Q˙\dot{Q}. The full lines present the fit curves according to Eq.(10). The corresponding parameters Q1Q_{1} and Pa​xP_{ax} are shown in Figs. 4 and 6 as a function of T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2}. Q1Q_{1} is evidently proportional to T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} for T1<3T_{1}<3K and one can estimate PQ=16.7×1044P_{Q}=16.7\times 10^{44} Jm3. At higher T1T_{1}, the results deviate from the linear dependence. However, no saturation of the heat release as a function of T1T_{1} is observed up to 2020 K, which is a typical behavior of anomalous TLSs. This is a clear indication that t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max}. At long time we observe a faster relaxation due to τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}. The additional contribution Pa​xP_{ax} determines the heat release far a long time. The energy dependence is similar to that for Q1Q_{1}. The parameter τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} is close to the corresponding values of PMMA with a similar energy dependence for low T1T_{1} (see Fig. 3).

Interesting results were obtained for this material by measuring the heat release as a function of the final temperature T0T_{0} (see Fig. 8). The variation in T0T_{0} from 1.6 K to 3.2 K does not influence the parameter τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}. However, a strong reduction of τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} is observed for T0>3.2T_{0}>3.2 K. This means that above 3.23.2 K the thermal activation process dominates, and we expect a saturation of the heat release as a function of T1T_{1} around 44 K provided that the barrier heights are constant. In fact, Q1Q_{1} is no more proportional to T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} for T1>3T_{1}>3 K (the heat release caused by normal TLSs saturates). However, no saturation is observed up to 2020 K which is a strong indication that the further increase of the heat release at T1>4T_{1}>4 K is caused by anomalous TLSs.

II.3 Heat capacity and heat release of PS

Heat release measurements in polystyrene were performed by Nittke et. al [17]. In the range of 0.70.7 h <t<<t< 66 h at T0=0.2T_{0}=0.2 K with 0.50.5 K <T1<<T_{1}< 11K measurments show that the heat release and Q1Q_{1} are proportional to t−1t^{-1} and T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2}, respectively (see Fig. 17 in [17]). Resulting PQ=9×1038P_{Q}=9\times 10^{38} J/g, is in a good agreement with PC=7.5×1038P_{C}=7.5\times 10^{38} J/g deduced from the heat capacity [17, 18]. All results are in perfect agreement with the STM and no contributions of anomalous TLSs was observed. Notice, however, that the heat release was measured for a quite short time and low T1T_{1} only. The contribution of anomalous TLSs would be much larger for high T1T_{1} and long time. Indeed, the heat release measured after cooling from 8080 K to 0.30.3 K in a wide time range shows the typical time dependence caused by the anomalous TLSs (see Fig. 9) with τam​a​x=60\tau_{a}^{max}=60 h.

II.4 Heat capacity and heat release of epoxy resin

The heat release of epoxy resin was measured after cooling from 292292 K to 1.151.15 K during 2525 days [19]. It was found to be proportional to t−0.76t^{-0.76} (see Fig. 9). A similar time dependence was found for epoxy glue Stycast [20]. Eq. (8) gives a good fit for epoxy with a very long τam​a​x=350\tau_{a}^{max}=350 h. At lower T1T_{1} the power law in the time dependence does not change: the relation between Q1Q_{1} and Pa​xP_{ax} is the same for different T1T_{1}. This holds only when both contributions are caused by anomalous TLSs. Q1Q_{1} deviates from the STM at T1>3T_{1}>3K (the saturation of the heat release caused by the normal TLSs) but the heat release is still increasing up to the highest temperature T1=22T_{1}=22 K. This is again a clear indication that the heat release is produced by anomalous TLSs.

The step in the distribution function was found for higher T0T_{0} in the thermally activated range [19] (see Fig. 10). Here the thermal absorption was measured after heating the sample from T1T_{1} to T0T_{0} (i.e. T1<T0T_{1}<T_{0}). Since the thermal activation alters the time dependence for shorter time as well, we fit the data by a power law

Q˙=P(t0)(t0/t)−aexp(−t/τam​a​x),\dot{Q}=P(t_{0})(t_{0}/t)^{-a}\exp(-t/\tau_{a}^{max}), (12)

where P⁡(t0)P(t_{0}) is the heat release at t=t0t=t_{0} (t0≪τam​a​xt_{0}\ll\tau_{a}^{max}) and the fit parameter aa depends on T0T_{0}. The parameter τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} changes rapidly with increasing temperature T0T_{0} from 33 h at 3.953.95 K to 5050 h at 2.232.23 K.

For a better understanding, Fig. 11 shows these data together with the calculated temperature dependencies within the STM. At the crossover temperature Tc​0=3T_{c0}=3 K the tunneling relaxation rate becomes equal to the rate of thermal activation. Thus the value of τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} at the lowest temperature lies in the tunneling range, while two others are in the range of thermal activation. The Arrhenius law τt​a−1=τ0−1exp(−V/kBT)\tau_{ta}^{-1}=\tau_{0}^{-1}\exp(-V/k_{B}T) with τ0=10−17\tau_{0}=10^{-17} s yields effective barrier heights Vm/kB=163V_{m}/k_{B}=163 K (T0=3.33T_{0}=3.33 K) of the TLSs causing at this time the heat. It is expected within the STM (where barrier heights are temperature independent) that the corresponding relaxation time decreases very rapidly with increasing temperature (see Fig. 11, dashed line). For normal tunneling systems this leads to the saturation of the heat release at the freezing temperature Tn∗T^{*}_{n}, which is about 20% higher than Tc​oT_{co}, i.e. Tn∗=3.6T^{*}_{n}=3.6 K. However, no saturation was found up to 2222 K (see Fig. 4). In addition, the measured τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} at 3.953.95 K is 33 orders of magnitude longer than expected from the Arrhenius law (open square in Fig. 11). All these facts demonstrate that the effective barrier height increases at higher temperature as shown in Fig. 12. Both the barrier height and the corresponding relaxation time in Fig. 11 were calculated with the following fit function (the curve in Fig. 12):

Vam​a​x/kB=[140+3300exp(−16.5K/T)]K.V^{max}_{a}/k_{B}=[140+3300\exp(-16.5\textrm{K}/T)]\textrm{K}. (13)

We can estimate the freezing temperature Ta∗=60T^{*}_{a}=60 K from the T12−T02T_{1}^{2}-T_{0}^{2} dependence of the parameter Q1Q_{1} in Fig. 4 by extrapolation of the experimental data at high and low T1T_{1}; finally we get from Eq. (8) in [1] the barrier height Vm/kB=2800V_{m}/k_{B}=2800 K, which is close to Vm​a​xV^{max}.

One can also estimate the maximum barrier height from the internal friction experiments. No maximum of the damping was observed in experiments with epoxy up to 100100 K (f=150f=150 MHz) [21]. This leads to a maximum barrier height larger than 18001800 K. A damping peak nearby 110110 K can be estimated for the TLSs in the vibrating reed experiments (f=84f=84 KHz) with stycast [22]. This yields Vm​a​x/kB=2860V^{max}/k_{B}=2860 K (full squares in Fig. 12). All these parameters are in a reasonable relation. Thus, the TLSs with the maximum barrier heights become frozen in state at 6060 K (open circles in Figs. 11 and 13) and their relaxation time increases with decreasing temperature, reaches a maximum value of 101810^{18} s at about 1515 K than returns to a short time 10410^{4} s at 44 K (see Fig. 13). Let us note that the Arrhenius law gives 1030310^{303} s (!) for the relaxation time of TLSs with the maximum barrier height at 44 K.

II.5 Heat release of pentanol-2

Pentanol is a good candidate for a proton target due to its high hydrogen content (C5H11OH). However, a high polarization requires an uniform distribution of the paramagnetic centers, which is much better in amorphous than crystalline materials. A standard cooling of pentanol with a dilution refrigerator yields polycrystalline pentanol. A difficult procedure was necessary to get the amorphous structure. The pentanol was mixed with 55 % water and cooled down rapidly by liquid nitrogen (the glass transition temperature TgT_{g} lies near 170170 K). Then the solid pentanol was mounted rapidly in the dilution refrigerator and cooled down to lower temperatures. This procedure is not too convenient. Therefore we check Pentanol-2, where the OH-group is transferred from the end of the long molecule to the side. Indeed, the worse symmetry of the molecules leads to an amorphous structure by normal cooling in a dilution refrigerator. Heat release experiments showed clearly a glassy behavior, however with deviations in the time dependence: the heat release was found to be proportional to t−0.69t^{-0.69} between 2020 and 500500 min [23]. Eq. (8) gives also a good fit of the time dependence. The corresponding parameters Q1Q_{1} are shown in Fig. 4. The crossover temperature is near 33 K and one expects a saturation within the STM above 44 K. However, the T1T_{1}-dependence does not saturate up to 1212 K. The data are close to that of epoxy resin (see Fig. 4).

III Discussion

We can make three main conclusions from the above-reviewed experimental data for amorphous organic materials:

  1. 1.

    The main contribution to the heat release comes from anomalous TLSs. Indeed, the heat release saturates at very high starting temperatures T1T_{1} (a giant heat release), the distribution parameter PQP_{Q} is close to PCP_{C} (or larger) and the heat release relaxes faster at very long time.

  2. 2.

    The heat release experiments with organic glasses correspond to the considered cases (1) and (2), where t≤τam​a​xt\leq\tau_{a}^{max}. In fact, τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} in organic glasses is longer than in inorganic ones or glasslike crystalline materials, except NbTi/D (see Fig. 3).

  3. 3.

    In contrast to inorganic materials, for a long time, but t<τam​a​xt<\tau_{a}^{max} the heat release is roughly proportional to t−at^{-a} with 0.5<a<0.80.5<a<0.8.

We also put emphasis on an abrupt decrease of the heat release with time in 3-mp/2,3-dmb, which cannot be described even by suggesting a cut in P⁡(V)P(V).

Let us analyse these conclusions with relation to the model of local mechanical deformations due to giant large-scale fluctuations in thermal expansion during the cooling of a sample [24]. According to this model, the thermal expansion coefficients α⁡(𝐫)\alpha(\bf r) take random values inside the dilatation centers of the sample. The dispersion in the distribution of α⁡(𝐫)\alpha(\bf r) is suggested to be much bigger than its mean value: ⟨α2⟩/⟨α⟩2∼[D/(Γ​Ea​v)]2∼105\langle\alpha^{2}\rangle/\langle\alpha\rangle^{2}\sim[D/(\Gamma E_{av})]^{2}\sim 10^{5}, where DD is the deformation potential, Γ\Gamma is the Grüneisen parameter. Rapid cooling from an initial temperature T1T_{1} to a final T0T_{0} results in a generation of strong local mechanical stresses, which provokes a linear reduction in the barrier height. As a consequence, the life time of high-energy TLSs reduces and their heat release becomes experimentally observable. Namely these TLSs are called anomalous.

This model allows us to explain qualitatively an increase of τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} with an average energy of TLSs Ea​vE_{av} (see Fig. 3). Indeed, the dispersion ⟨α2⟩\langle\alpha^{2}\rangle decreases when T0+T1T_{0}+T_{1} grows. This results in growing barrier heights of anomalous TLSs, reducing of Δ0\Delta_{0}, and increasing relaxation time. Regarding the second item of our conclusions, the edge in the distribution function of anomalous TLSs is shifted to the left against the edge of normal TLSs on the value Δ​V=∓σ​Va​c\Delta V=\mp\sigma V_{ac}. This step can be explained under the assumption of a fixed limit of local stresses σm​a​x\sigma^{max}. Taking into account the structural characteristics of the materials one can suggest that σm​a​x\sigma^{max} has a maximal value for inorganic crystalls, a little lesser for amorphous materials and has a smaller value for organic polymers. Indeed, the corresponding inverse behavior of τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} takes place (see Fig. 3).

Deviations from the t−1t^{-1} behavior in the heat release can be related to the increase of the spectral density P0​(t)∼t1−aP_{0}(t)\sim t^{1-a} during the cooling process. This means a gradual increase of local stresses and/or sizes of stress concentrated regions. In the last case, an increase of P0P_{0} will be accompanied by a shift of Vm​a​xV^{max} to the left. This can explain an abrupt decrease of Q˙​(t)\dot{Q}(t) in 3-mp/2,3-dmb.

It should be stressed that there is no evidence of any deviations from t−1t^{-1} behavior in the heat release in inorganic materials. Therefore, a suggested increase of local stresses should be a specific property of organic materials. We suppose that local stresses are influenced by an expansion of the sample during the heat release process. Indeed, an average thermal expansion coefficient ⟨α⟩\langle\alpha\rangle is related to CpC_{p}, Grüneisen parameter Γ\Gamma and isothermal compressibility κT\kappa_{T} as

⟨α⟩=κT​Γ​Cp.\langle\alpha\rangle=\kappa_{T}\Gamma C_{p}. (14)

According to (4), the heat capacity grows with time. At the same time, in organic polymers κT\kappa_{T} and τm​i​n\tau^{min} have a several orders bigger and lesser values, respectively, in comparison to the inorganic materials. A decrease of τm​i​n\tau^{min} is a result of strong electron-phonon interactions in polymers. Hence in polymers we can expect a more pronounced influence of ⟨α⟩\langle\alpha\rangle. Even a slow drift of ⟨α⟩\langle\alpha\rangle can provoke a formation of additional local stresses and, as a consequence, a raising quantity of anomalous TLSs.

As another possible explanation of this phenomenon (which would also approve Eq. (8)) one can suggest the existence of an unknown additional channel which provides the relaxation of TLSs in the time τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max} independently of the barrier heights. Unfortunately, the origin of this sort of TLS relaxation is still an open question. A possible candidate is the resonant relaxation based on TLS-TLS interaction at very low temperatures suggested in  [14].

IV Summary

Summarising, our analysis shows that all glasses (amorphous organic, inorganic, and glasslike crystalline materials) reveal an universal behavior of the relation between the heat release and the heat capacity in good agreement with our model of anomalous TLSs (see Table 1). The heat release shows a similar behavior in various organic polymers and has some peculiar properties in comparison with inorganic glasses and glasslike crystals. We have shown that despite these peculiarities all existing heat release data can be explained within the model of local mechanical stresses where specific properties of organic polymers are caused by a lower value of the maximum stress and a more pronounced drift of an average thermal expansion coefficient due to a bigger value of isothermal compressibility and stronger electron-phonon interaction. It should be stressed that organic glasses are convenient for further experimental investigations of the giant heat release owing to their longer τam​a​x\tau_{a}^{max}.
